scientific_analysis.disease_focus_rationale: The document's own content (title, abstract, methods, results) is entirely about caregiver burden in dementia patients under Private Nursing Services in Qatar, measured with the Zarit Burden Interview; it contains no mention of Lyme disease or Long COVID, so the schema's lyme/long_covid/both categories do not apply and the locally detected 'dementia' focus is confirmed, not corrected to either of the two in-scope conditions.
scientific_analysis.plain_language_summary: This is a cross-sectional survey study of 101 caregivers (out of 146 approached) of dementia patients cared for under Qatar's Private Nursing Services program at Hamad Medical Corporation. Using the 22-item Zarit Burden Interview (ZBI), it measures the physical, emotional, social, and financial burden these caregivers report, finding an average burden score of 42.8 (SD 19.6) on a 0-88 scale, with 36.6% experiencing moderate-to-severe burden and 18.8% severe burden. Burden was statistically associated with lower education and spousal relationship to the patient, while gender, age, nationality, living arrangement, and caregiving hours per day did not show a statistically significant association in this sample. The study reports no dollar costs, no direct medical expenditure data, and no data on diagnostic delay or insurance/access barriers; its burden measure is a composite psychometric score, not a monetary figure.

Loss of personal space/privacy and strained social relationships are discussed narratively as stressors.
Risk of caregiver burnout from 16-24h/day caregiving is raised as a concern in the Discussion even though the corresponding statistical test (hours/day vs. burden) did not reach significance.
Policy and recommendation sections mention respite care, counseling, financial subsidies, and flexible work policies as proposed (not currently implemented or measured) supports.
evidence_gaps: No direct medical cost or private-nursing-service fee data are reported anywhere in the document.
No indirect-cost data (lost wages, income loss, employment/productivity impact) in monetary terms are reported, despite 'financial instability' being named as a stressor.
No data on diagnostic delay, care-seeking pathways, or insurance/access barriers for dementia patients or their caregivers are reported.
Cross-sectional design precludes tracking burden or cost change over time or assessing long-term financial consequences, as the authors themselves note.
Caregiver resilience, coping style, and social support were not assessed, which the authors state are established predictors of burden.
No adjustment was made for dementia severity, behavioral symptoms, or patient functional status, as the authors state in their own Limitations section.
comparison_boundaries: This is a single cross-sectional sample of 101 caregivers surveyed under one specific nursing-service program (PNS, Hamad Medical Corporation, Qatar); its findings should not be pooled with the Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, or UAE studies cited in the Discussion, since those are separate studies with their own populations, instruments, and methods used only as narrative comparators, not merged data sources.
The ZBI total score (0-88 ordinal composite) is a psychometric burden score, not a monetary cost estimate, and must not be rescaled or treated as a dollar figure.

Subgroup percentages in Table 3 (by education, relationship, gender, hours/day) are drawn from small cell counts (e.g., n=13 spouses, n=19 in the severe-burden group); these should not be treated as precise population-level rates or pooled across cells.

101 of 146 approached caregivers completed the survey (69.1% response rate); results describe only the completing subsample and should not be extrapolated as representing all 146 PNS dementia patients/caregivers without acknowledging possible nonresponse bias.
The document reports no price year or dollar figures at all, so there is no cost basis available for any cross-year or cross-currency comparison.

sex_gender_findings.finding: The document reports caregiver composition and burden broken out by gender: 75.2% of the 101 caregivers were female overall, and Table 3 shows female caregivers comprised 80% of the minimal-burden group, 67% of moderate, 76% of moderate-to-severe, and 84% of severe-burden groups, but this gender difference in burden category did not reach statistical significance (p=0.53 vs. the study's own p<0.05 threshold).

scale_findings.quote: The average ZBI score of 42.8 ± 19.6 indicates moderate to severe caregiving challenges.

decision_relevance.summary: A simulator built from this document could help dementia-program administrators and policymakers in Qatar (e.g., Hamad Medical Corporation's Private Nursing Services, the Ministry of Public Health, or planners of the National Dementia Plan) understand which caregiver subgroups report the highest ZBI-measured burden and target support resources accordingly. Because the document reports a psychometric burden score and subgroup associations rather than dollar costs, the simulator's usefulness is limited to burden-severity and service-targeting questions, not cost-of-illness estimation. It cannot answer questions about direct medical costs, lost income, or long-term financial consequences, since the document does not quantify these.
use_cases: Program administrators at Qatar's Private Nursing Services could use the ZBI subgroup findings (spousal caregivers at 37% severe burden, lower-education caregivers at higher moderate-to-severe burden) to prioritize which caregiver groups are offered respite care or counseling referrals first.

Policy planners revising Qatar's National Dementia Plan could use the reported overall burden prevalence (36.6% moderate-to-severe, 18.8% severe among 101 surveyed caregivers) to gauge the scale of caregiver support services potentially needed, while recognizing this reflects a psychometric burden score and a single-program sample, not a cost or national prevalence estimate.

spec.title: Dementia Caregiver Burden Simulator (Qatar Private Nursing Services, Zarit Burden Interview)
spec.boundary: This simulation represents a single cross-sectional survey of 101 caregivers (69.1% of 146 approached) of dementia patients under Qatar's Private Nursing Services (PNS) program at Hamad Medical Corporation, measured with the 22-item Zarit Burden Interview (ZBI, scored 0-88, higher = more burden). It covers overall burden prevalence and the two subgroup associations the study found statistically significant: spousal relationship to the patient (p=0.011) and lower caregiver education (p=0.019). The document also reports that gender (75.2% of caregivers were female) and caregiving hours per day were NOT significantly associated with burden category in this sample (p=0.53 and p=0.32 respectively) - these non-significant findings are kept visible rather than implied away. This simulation does NOT represent any dollar cost, income loss, diagnostic delay, or access-barrier data, because the source document reports none of these; it is a psychometric burden score study, not a cost-of-illness study, and its findings come from one program in one country and should not be generalized nationally or pooled with other countries' studies.

takeaway.patient: A study of 101 caregivers looking after dementia patients under a nursing-support program in Qatar used a standard caregiving-stress questionnaire (the Zarit Burden Interview, scored 0 to 88, where higher means more burden) and found an average score of about 43, with roughly a third of caregivers in the moderate-to-severe range and about a fifth in the severe range. Caregivers who were the patient's spouse, and caregivers with less formal education, reported noticeably higher burden than other caregivers in this same sample. The study did not measure any dollar costs, but it did report that about 1 in 5 caregivers worried they would not have enough money to keep providing care.
takeaway.care: Among 101 caregivers surveyed in one dementia nursing-support program, roughly a third screened into moderate-to-severe burden and about a fifth into severe burden on the ZBI, with spousal caregivers and lower-education caregivers showing significantly higher burden than other subgroups in this sample; caregiving hours per day and caregiver gender did not show a significant association with burden level here. The study also notes an internal inconsistency in its own reported caregiving-duration figures (5.6 years in the text vs. 2.6 years in its own table) that it does not resolve.
takeaway.policy: In this single-program, cross-sectional sample (101 of 146 approached caregivers, 69.1% response), 36.6% of dementia caregivers under Qatar's Private Nursing Services reported moderate-to-severe burden and 18.8% reported severe burden on the Zarit Burden Interview, with spousal relationship and lower education significantly associated with higher burden (gender and caregiving-hours associations were not significant here). The study reports no cost data, so it can inform service-targeting and need-scale discussions for this specific program but cannot support cost-effectiveness or national-prevalence conclusions.

patient: If you are a spousal caregiver, this study found spouses reported the highest caregiving burden among the groups surveyed - this may be worth raising with your care team as a reason to ask about respite care or counseling support.

If financial worry about sustaining care resonates with you, note that the study found about 1 in 5 caregivers shared that concern - consider asking your program about any financial-support or subsidy options, since the study itself did not measure actual costs.

The burden score described here (0-88) reflects emotional and physical strain, not your or your family member's medical condition - a high score is about your own caregiving load, which is something you can mention when asking for more support.
care: Consider using the spousal-caregiver and lower-education subgroup findings to prioritize early referral to respite care or counseling, since these were the only two subgroups where this study found a statistically significant burden association.

Caregiving hours per day (including the 43.6% providing 16-24 hours daily) did not show a significant link to ZBI burden score in this sample - this may be worth checking against your own caseload before assuming hour-count alone predicts who needs support.

This study's own reported caregiving-duration figures are inconsistent (5.6 years in text vs. 2.6 years in its table) - this discrepancy may be worth flagging if using this study's duration statistic for planning purposes.

Routine ZBI screening at intake, alongside relationship-to-patient and education level, could help flag caregivers for proactive outreach, consistent with the two subgroups this study found most at risk.
policy: Use the reported moderate-to-severe (36.6%) and severe (18.8%) burden prevalence, within this 101-caregiver surveyed subsample, to gauge the potential scale of respite-care and counseling needs for this specific nursing-service program, not as a national prevalence estimate.

Given the significant spousal and education-level associations found here, consider whether support programs (financial subsidies, flexible work policies, counseling) the study's Discussion proposes could be piloted first for these two subgroups.

Because this study reports no direct cost or income-loss data, commissioning a companion cost-of-illness study specific to this caregiver population would be needed before any cost-based policy decisions.

Given the 69.1% response rate and single-program, single-country design, avoid pooling these prevalence figures with the Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, or UAE studies cited in the document without separately re-analyzing comparable data.

inputs.label: Mean Zarit Burden Interview score
inputs.source: Document Abstract/Results/Table 2 reports a mean ZBI score of 42.8 (SD 19.6); the 0-88 min/max reflects the document's own description of the full ZBI scale range, not a chosen exploration bound.
inputs.interpretation: This is the document's reported average caregiver burden score across all 101 surveyed caregivers on the 0-88 ZBI scale; moving it explores how a different average overall burden level would compare to what the document found, independent of the subgroup gaps below.

inputs.label: Moderate-to-severe burden prevalence
inputs.source: Document Abstract states 36.6% of caregivers experienced moderate-to-severe burden; the 0-100 range is an assumed exploration bound (the natural range for a percentage), not document-specified.
inputs.interpretation: This is the share of the 101 surveyed caregivers whose ZBI score placed them in the moderate-to-severe burden category; a higher value means more of this sample reported substantial caregiving strain.

inputs.label: Severe burden prevalence
inputs.source: Document Abstract/Results/Table 2 states 18.8% faced severe caregiving challenges; the 0-100 range is an assumed exploration bound, not document-specified.
inputs.interpretation: This is the share of surveyed caregivers at the most severe ZBI burden level; it feeds the spousal-versus-overall severe-burden gap output below.

inputs.label: Severe burden prevalence among spousal caregivers
inputs.source: Document Discussion/Table 3 reports 37% of spousal caregivers (a subgroup of n=13 within the 101 surveyed) reported severe burden, associated with relationship-to-patient (p=0.011); the 0-100 range is an assumed exploration bound.
inputs.interpretation: This is the severe-burden prevalence specifically among spousal caregivers, the subgroup the document identifies as most burdened; moving it changes the spousal-vs-overall gap output, which is the document's key significant relationship finding.

inputs.label: Minimal burden prevalence, graduate-or-above education
inputs.source: Document Results/Table 3 reports 73% of caregivers with graduate or higher education experienced minimal burden, associated with education level (p=0.019); the 0-100 range is an assumed exploration bound.
inputs.interpretation: This is the minimal-burden prevalence among the most-educated caregiver subgroup; it feeds the education-level burden gap output and lets you see how that gap would change if this subgroup's minimal-burden rate were different.

inputs.label: Minimal burden prevalence, secondary education
inputs.source: Document Results/Table 3 reports 26% of secondary-educated caregivers experienced minimal burden, associated with education level (p=0.019); the 0-100 range is an assumed exploration bound.
inputs.interpretation: This is the minimal-burden prevalence among the least-educated caregiver subgroup in the sample; it is the comparator for the education-level burden gap output.

outputs.label: Mean caregiver burden score
outputs.interpretation: This reproduces the document's reported average ZBI burden score among the 101 surveyed caregivers; the document describes an average in this range as reflecting moderate-to-severe caregiving challenges overall, with higher scores meaning greater reported burden.

outputs.label: Moderate-to-severe burden prevalence
outputs.interpretation: This is the share of the 101 surveyed caregivers who fell into the moderate-to-severe ZBI category; a higher value means more of this sample reported substantial caregiving burden, a lower value means less.

outputs.label: Severe burden prevalence
outputs.interpretation: This is the share of surveyed caregivers who fell into the most severe ZBI burden category; a higher value means more of this sample reported the most intense caregiving strain measured by this instrument.

outputs.label: Spousal-minus-overall severe burden gap (positive = spousal caregivers more often severe; negative = less often)
outputs.interpretation: This is the percentage-point difference between spousal caregivers' severe-burden prevalence and the severe-burden prevalence across all surveyed caregivers. The document found spouses had the highest severe-burden share, a statistically significant association (p=0.011) in this sample; this output is an illustrative arithmetic comparison and moving the inputs does not itself re-test that association.

outputs.label: Graduate-minus-secondary minimal burden gap (positive = graduate-educated caregivers more often minimal burden; negative = less often)
outputs.interpretation: This is the percentage-point difference in minimal-burden prevalence between graduate-or-above-educated and secondary-educated caregivers. The document found education level significantly associated with burden category (p=0.019) in this sample, with more-educated caregivers more often reporting minimal burden; this output is an illustrative arithmetic comparison, not a re-test of that association.

scenarios.label: Spousal caregiver severe-burden rate
scenarios.goal: Shows how severe-burden prevalence compares between the overall sample and spousal caregivers.
scenarios.description: Replaces the overall severe-burden prevalence (18.8%) with the rate the study reports specifically among its 13 spousal caregivers (37%), an observational subgroup comparison the document reports side by side, not a causal claim.

scenarios.label: Secondary-education caregiver pattern
scenarios.goal: Shows how minimal-burden prevalence would look if graduate-educated caregivers matched the secondary-education group's rate.
scenarios.description: Substitutes the secondary-education minimal-burden rate (26%) reported in the same table for the graduate-education input's default (73%), an observational subgroup comparison, not a causal claim.

scenarios.label: Graduate-education caregiver pattern
scenarios.goal: Shows how minimal-burden prevalence would look if secondary-educated caregivers matched the graduate-education group's rate.
scenarios.description: Substitutes the graduate-education minimal-burden rate (73%) reported in the same table for the secondary-education input's default (26%), an observational subgroup comparison, not a causal claim.

package.documentation:
## Source and design
This simulator is built from a peer-reviewed cross-sectional survey of 101 caregivers (69.1% of 146 approached) of dementia patients cared for under Qatar's Private Nursing Services (PNS) program at Hamad Medical Corporation. Burden was measured with the 22-item Zarit Burden Interview (ZBI), a 0-88 composite score where higher values indicate more caregiving strain.

## What the inputs and outputs represent
All figures are observed survey statistics, not costs: the mean ZBI score (42.8, SD 19.6), the share of caregivers in the moderate-to-severe burden category (36.6%), and the share in the severe category (18.8%). Two subgroup findings reached statistical significance in this sample: spousal caregivers (a subgroup of n=13) had the highest severe-burden prevalence (37%), associated with relationship to the patient (p=0.011); and caregiver education level was associated with burden (p=0.019), with 73% of graduate-or-above-educated caregivers reporting minimal burden versus 26% of secondary-educated caregivers. These two gaps are modeled as simple percentage-point differences for illustrative comparison only; they do not re-test or strengthen the underlying statistical finding.

## Sex/gender and non-significant findings
75.2% of the 101 caregivers were female. The document reports that burden category did not differ significantly by gender (p=0.53) or by caregiving hours per day (p=0.32, despite 43.6% of caregivers providing 16-24 hours of care daily) in this sample; these non-significant associations are noted here rather than omitted.

## What is not modeled
The document reports no dollar cost, income-loss, or out-of-pocket spending figures, despite naming financial instability as a stressor (22% of caregivers feared insufficient resources to sustain care). No diagnostic-delay, access-barrier, or insurance data appear. The cross-sectional design precludes tracking burden change over time, and the authors themselves note no adjustment was made for dementia severity, behavioral symptoms, caregiver resilience, or social support.

## Known limitation in the source itself
The document's own reported mean caregiving duration is inconsistent: the Results text states 5.6 years (SD 4.8) while its own Table 1 lists 2.6 years (SD 4.8) for the same labeled variable. This simulator does not attempt to resolve that discrepancy.

## Generalizability
Findings describe only this 101-caregiver completing subsample within one nursing-service program in Qatar; subgroup percentages draw on small cells (e.g., n=13 spouses) and should not be treated as precise population rates, pooled with the Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, or UAE studies cited narratively in the source, or extrapolated to all 146 PNS patients/caregivers.

spec.title: Dementia Caregiver Burden Simulator (Qatar Private Nursing Services, Zarit Burden Interview)
spec.boundary: This simulation represents a single cross-sectional survey of 101 caregivers (69.1% of 146 approached) of dementia patients under Qatar's Private Nursing Services (PNS) program at Hamad Medical Corporation, measured with the 22-item Zarit Burden Interview (ZBI, scored 0-88, higher = more burden). It covers overall burden prevalence and the two subgroup associations the study found statistically significant: spousal relationship to the patient (p=0.011) and lower caregiver education (p=0.019). The document also reports that gender (75.2% of caregivers were female) and caregiving hours per day were NOT significantly associated with burden category in this sample (p=0.53 and p=0.32 respectively) - these non-significant findings are kept visible rather than implied away. This simulation does NOT represent any dollar cost, income loss, diagnostic delay, or access-barrier data, because the source document reports none of these; it is a psychometric burden score study, not a cost-of-illness study, and its findings come from one program in one country and should not be generalized nationally or pooled with other countries' studies.

takeaway.patient: A study of 101 caregivers looking after dementia patients under a nursing-support program in Qatar used a standard caregiving-stress questionnaire (the Zarit Burden Interview, scored 0 to 88, where higher means more burden) and found an average score of about 43, with roughly a third of caregivers in the moderate-to-severe range and about a fifth in the severe range. Caregivers who were the patient's spouse, and caregivers with less formal education, reported noticeably higher burden than other caregivers in this same sample. The study did not measure any dollar costs, but it did report that about 1 in 5 caregivers worried they would not have enough money to keep providing care.
takeaway.care: Among 101 caregivers surveyed in one dementia nursing-support program, roughly a third screened into moderate-to-severe burden and about a fifth into severe burden on the ZBI, with spousal caregivers and lower-education caregivers showing significantly higher burden than other subgroups in this sample; caregiving hours per day and caregiver gender did not show a significant association with burden level here. The study also notes an internal inconsistency in its own reported caregiving-duration figures (5.6 years in the text vs. 2.6 years in its own table) that it does not resolve.
takeaway.policy: In this single-program, cross-sectional sample (101 of 146 approached caregivers, 69.1% response), 36.6% of dementia caregivers under Qatar's Private Nursing Services reported moderate-to-severe burden and 18.8% reported severe burden on the Zarit Burden Interview, with spousal relationship and lower education significantly associated with higher burden (gender and caregiving-hours associations were not significant here). The study reports no cost data, so it can inform service-targeting and need-scale discussions for this specific program but cannot support cost-effectiveness or national-prevalence conclusions.

patient: If you are a spousal caregiver, this study found spouses reported the highest caregiving burden among the groups surveyed - this may be worth raising with your care team as a reason to ask about respite care or counseling support.

If financial worry about sustaining care resonates with you, note that the study found about 1 in 5 caregivers shared that concern - consider asking your program about any financial-support or subsidy options, since the study itself did not measure actual costs.

The burden score described here (0-88) reflects emotional and physical strain, not your or your family member's medical condition - a high score is about your own caregiving load, which is something you can mention when asking for more support.
care: Consider using the spousal-caregiver and lower-education subgroup findings to prioritize early referral to respite care or counseling, since these were the only two subgroups where this study found a statistically significant burden association.

Caregiving hours per day (including the 43.6% providing 16-24 hours daily) did not show a significant link to ZBI burden score in this sample - this may be worth checking against your own caseload before assuming hour-count alone predicts who needs support.

This study's own reported caregiving-duration figures are inconsistent (5.6 years in text vs. 2.6 years in its table) - this discrepancy may be worth flagging if using this study's duration statistic for planning purposes.

Routine ZBI screening at intake, alongside relationship-to-patient and education level, could help flag caregivers for proactive outreach, consistent with the two subgroups this study found most at risk.
policy: Use the reported moderate-to-severe (36.6%) and severe (18.8%) burden prevalence, within this 101-caregiver surveyed subsample, to gauge the potential scale of respite-care and counseling needs for this specific nursing-service program, not as a national prevalence estimate.

Given the significant spousal and education-level associations found here, consider whether support programs (financial subsidies, flexible work policies, counseling) the study's Discussion proposes could be piloted first for these two subgroups.

Because this study reports no direct cost or income-loss data, commissioning a companion cost-of-illness study specific to this caregiver population would be needed before any cost-based policy decisions.

Given the 69.1% response rate and single-program, single-country design, avoid pooling these prevalence figures with the Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, or UAE studies cited in the document without separately re-analyzing comparable data.

inputs.label: Mean Zarit Burden Interview score
inputs.source: Document Abstract/Results/Table 2 reports a mean ZBI score of 42.8 (SD 19.6); the 0-88 min/max reflects the document's own description of the full ZBI scale range, not a chosen exploration bound.
inputs.interpretation: This is the document's reported average caregiver burden score across all 101 surveyed caregivers on the 0-88 ZBI scale; moving it explores how a different average overall burden level would compare to what the document found, independent of the subgroup gaps below.

inputs.label: Moderate-to-severe burden prevalence
inputs.source: Document Abstract states 36.6% of caregivers experienced moderate-to-severe burden; the 0-100 range is an assumed exploration bound (the natural range for a percentage), not document-specified.
inputs.interpretation: This is the share of the 101 surveyed caregivers whose ZBI score placed them in the moderate-to-severe burden category; a higher value means more of this sample reported substantial caregiving strain.

inputs.label: Severe burden prevalence
inputs.source: Document Abstract/Results/Table 2 states 18.8% faced severe caregiving challenges; the 0-100 range is an assumed exploration bound, not document-specified.
inputs.interpretation: This is the share of surveyed caregivers at the most severe ZBI burden level; it feeds the spousal-versus-overall severe-burden gap output below.

inputs.label: Severe burden prevalence among spousal caregivers
inputs.source: Document Discussion/Table 3 reports 37% of spousal caregivers (a subgroup of n=13 within the 101 surveyed) reported severe burden, associated with relationship-to-patient (p=0.011); the 0-100 range is an assumed exploration bound.
inputs.interpretation: This is the severe-burden prevalence specifically among spousal caregivers, the subgroup the document identifies as most burdened; moving it changes the spousal-vs-overall gap output, which is the document's key significant relationship finding.

inputs.label: Minimal burden prevalence, graduate-or-above education
inputs.source: Document Results/Table 3 reports 73% of caregivers with graduate or higher education experienced minimal burden, associated with education level (p=0.019); the 0-100 range is an assumed exploration bound.
inputs.interpretation: This is the minimal-burden prevalence among the most-educated caregiver subgroup; it feeds the education-level burden gap output and lets you see how that gap would change if this subgroup's minimal-burden rate were different.

inputs.label: Minimal burden prevalence, secondary education
inputs.source: Document Results/Table 3 reports 26% of secondary-educated caregivers experienced minimal burden, associated with education level (p=0.019); the 0-100 range is an assumed exploration bound.
inputs.interpretation: This is the minimal-burden prevalence among the least-educated caregiver subgroup in the sample; it is the comparator for the education-level burden gap output.

outputs.label: Mean caregiver burden score
outputs.interpretation: This reproduces the document's reported average ZBI burden score among the 101 surveyed caregivers; the document describes an average in this range as reflecting moderate-to-severe caregiving challenges overall, with higher scores meaning greater reported burden.

outputs.label: Moderate-to-severe burden prevalence
outputs.interpretation: This is the share of the 101 surveyed caregivers who fell into the moderate-to-severe ZBI category; a higher value means more of this sample reported substantial caregiving burden, a lower value means less.

outputs.label: Severe burden prevalence
outputs.interpretation: This is the share of surveyed caregivers who fell into the most severe ZBI burden category; a higher value means more of this sample reported the most intense caregiving strain measured by this instrument.

outputs.label: Spousal-minus-overall severe burden gap (positive = spousal caregivers more often severe; negative = less often)
outputs.interpretation: This is the percentage-point difference between spousal caregivers' severe-burden prevalence and the severe-burden prevalence across all surveyed caregivers. The document found spouses had the highest severe-burden share, a statistically significant association (p=0.011) in this sample; this output is an illustrative arithmetic comparison and moving the inputs does not itself re-test that association.

outputs.label: Graduate-minus-secondary minimal burden gap (positive = graduate-educated caregivers more often minimal burden; negative = less often)
outputs.interpretation: This is the percentage-point difference in minimal-burden prevalence between graduate-or-above-educated and secondary-educated caregivers. The document found education level significantly associated with burden category (p=0.019) in this sample, with more-educated caregivers more often reporting minimal burden; this output is an illustrative arithmetic comparison, not a re-test of that association.

scenarios.label: Spousal caregiver severe-burden rate
scenarios.goal: Shows how severe-burden prevalence compares between the overall sample and spousal caregivers.
scenarios.description: Replaces the overall severe-burden prevalence (18.8%) with the rate the study reports specifically among its 13 spousal caregivers (37%), an observational subgroup comparison the document reports side by side, not a causal claim.

scenarios.goal: Shows how minimal-burden prevalence would look if graduate-educated caregivers matched the secondary-education group's rate.
scenarios.description: Substitutes the secondary-education minimal-burden rate (26%) reported in the same table for the graduate-education input's default (73%), an observational subgroup comparison, not a causal claim.
